shift-direction.question: The graph of $y=f(x-3)$ is the graph of $y=f(x)$ moved. Which way does it move?
shift-direction.explanation: The new graph gives the value $f(0)$ at $x=3$, because $3-3=0$. So the point that was at $x=0$ is now at $x=3$, and every point moves 3 units to the right. The minus sign makes the shift look backwards, but it is not.
optionFeedback: That is the shift for $f(x+3)$, where the plus sign is inside the brackets.
A shift up needs a number added outside the function, as in $f(x)+3$.
A shift down needs a number subtracted outside the function, as in $f(x)-3$.

shifted-value.question: Suppose $f(2)=5$ and let $g(x)=f(x-3)$. What is $g(5)$?
shifted-value.explanation: $g(5)=f(5-3)=f(2)=5$. The point $(2,5)$ on the graph of $f$ moves 3 units to the right and becomes the point $(5,5)$ on the graph of $g$.

reflect-inside.question: In general, how does the graph of $y=f(-x)$ compare with the graph of $y=f(x)$?
options: It is shifted to the left
reflect-inside.explanation: The minus sign is inside the brackets, so it changes the input. The point $(2,f(2))$ on the graph of $f$ gives the point $(-2,f(2))$ on the new graph: the height stays the same and the point moves to the other side of the $y$-axis. A minus sign outside, as in $-f(x)$, flips the height instead and reflects in the $x$-axis.
